Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PA View image in fullscreen Nirmal Purja had been leading an expedition on Broad Peak along with climbers from Nepal, Pakistan, Oman, China and the US. Photograph: Nirmal Purja/PA Mountaineering World-renowned climber Nirmal Purja among 11 struck by avalanche on Pakistan mountain Rescuers say four bodies found in search for team caught in Broad Peak avalanche, after trackers showed rapid descent Peter Beaumont and Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad Fri 31 Jul 2026 11.35 EDT First published on Thu 30 Jul 2026 22.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The world-renowned Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja – a former British special forces member – is among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak. The Alpine Club of Pakistan said “seven climbers have been spotted via aerial drone footage” adding that “their identities and condition cannot yet be verified”. Rescuers had said earlier on Friday that four bodies had been found and efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Three of the dead have been identified: Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepali citizen, Nadhira Alharthy, who was the first Omani to climb Everest, and US climber Mallory Geis. Their bodies have been transported to a hospital. Purja, also known as Nims Dai, made history in 2019 after climbing all of the world’s 14 peaks over 8,000 metres in just over six months, cutting years off the previous record. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain in winter, a highly coveted achievement. View image in fullscreen Nirmal ‘Nims’ Purja and his Project Possible team are congratulated after successfully scaling all 14 mountains above 8,000 metres in just over six months. Photograph: Skanda Gautam/Zuma Wire/Rex/Shutterstock Purja has also attracted controversy, however, including a high-profile claim, which he denied , of sexually inappropriate behaviour. Also among those missing are the US climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese national, Wang Zhong, and Pakistani and Nepali high-altitude workers. As night fell on the mountain on Friday, visual searches for any survivors, including with the use of drones, were halted. Search efforts have been hampered by the weather and the fact that unlike in Nepal, where there is a well-established network of private helicopter search and rescue operations, helicopters are less available in Pakistan and run by the military. Map showing location of Broad Peak Trackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camp two and camp three on the mountain’s west ridge, the most popular ascent route. According to Climbing magazine , Geis’s tracker showed a sudden descent of 543 metres, while Alharthy’s tracker showed a much-larger descent of 1,651 metres. View image in fullscreen Broad Peak, on the border of Pakistan and China, is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,047 metres. Photograph: Naveed Hussain/Alamy Commenting on the rescue efforts, a spokesperson for police in the mountainous Gilgit-Baltistan region said “preliminary reports indicate that four bodies have so far been recovered”, adding that the condition of the remaining climbers was still being verified. A statement by the Alpine Club of Pakistan (ACP) suggested an avalanche had struck a group of climbers around midday on Thursday. “The entire team has been out of communication since the avalanche,” the statement said, as teams with helicopters and drones were sent to help with rescue efforts. The statement added: “Every possible effort is being made to ensure that helicopter support and all available rescue resources are mobilised at the earliest opportunity, subject to weather and operational conditions.” Irfan Arshad Khan, the ACP’s president, said: “We can confirm the death of three climbers, as we received two dead bodies and a body part of another climber.” Purja’s business partner, Mingma Gyabu Sherpa, who is also a member of the Nepali house of representatives, said data appeared to show continuing movement from Purja’s tracking device after the initial incident. “Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche,” he told the Nepali news site Kantipur. “But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again.” Mingma added that one Pakistani and one Nepali climber had set out overland towards the suspected avalanche site to check reports that one climber’s location appeared to be near the base of the mountain. “We have received information that one person’s location appears to be near the foot of the mountain. A search team has gone there to verify it,” he said. Mingma cautioned that they did not have any indication of Purja’s condition, simply that the location of the tracker had shifted. In person, Purja was striking for his confidence and self-belief . His rapid chain of ascents of the world’s tallest mountains demonstrated strength and a talent for logistical organisation, using the exploit to showcase what he felt were the overlooked abilities of Nepali climbers. His profile was boosted after he starred in a 2021 Netflix documentary on the feat. The previous record for climbing all 14 was seven years; his record was surpassed in 2023. View image in fullscreen Purja, after being part of the all-Nepali mountaineering team that became the first to scale K2 in winter, arrives at Tribhuwan international airport in Kathmandu in January 2021. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Purja was leading an expedition for his company, Elite Exped, on Broad Peak, the world’s 12th-highest mountain at 8,047 metres, when the avalanche occurred. The ACP received “deeply concerning” reports on Thursday that an avalanche had struck the team. ‘It’s not about ego’, says speed climber who tamed world’s 14 highest peaks Read more The expedition includes five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said the ACP’s vice-president, Karrar Haidri. “The club prays for the safety and successful rescue of all the climbers and stands in solidarity with their families and the international mountaineering community during this difficult time,” the ACP said in a statement. View image in fullscreen Nims Purja on Manaslu, the world’s eighth-highest mountain, in Nepal Photograph: Supplied Purja, who is also a British citizen after joining the British army in 2003, opted to use supplementary oxygen for his ascents, justifying his choice by the huge size of the challenge he had set himself. Purja had written on X this week that he was close to becoming the first person to climb all 14 mountains over 8,000 metres twice without oxygen. “Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down,” he wrote. “I take zero mountains for granted. Not one. The moment my foot leaves basecamp, it’s 100%. Always has been. Always will be. “My purpose has never been about me. It’s about what I represent. It’s about showing YOU that your own mountains – whatever they are – are climbable.” Explore more on these topics Mountaineering Pakistan Nepal Oman China South and central Asia Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/music/2026/a.text: Fans of singer Bonnie Tyler line the streets as her coffin is taken back to her former home ahead of her funeral, in Mumbles, Wales. Photograph: Alastair Grant/AP View image in fullscreen Fans of singer Bonnie Tyler line the streets as her coffin is taken back to her former home ahead of her funeral, in Mumbles, Wales. Photograph: Alastair Grant/AP Bonnie Tyler Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans gather to pay respects as coffin brought home Fans line streets, singing Total Eclipse of the Heart ahead of Welsh singer’s Swansea funeral Aneesa Ahmed Sat 15 Aug 2026 14.44 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 17.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans lined the streets of her home town in south Wales to pay respects to the singer as her coffin was brought back to her former home. The singer, whose real name was Gaynor Sullivan, died unexpectedly on 8 July in Portugal at the age of 75. Many fans stood along Newton Road in Mumbles, Swansea , to watch the procession as her coffin was brought back. The coffin was draped in the Welsh flag and accompanied by a framed photograph of the singer. View image in fullscreen Fans pay their respects by placing flowers on the hearse carrying Welsh singer Bonnie Tyler as it travels along Newton Road to her home in Llwynderw, Mumbles, Wales. Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPA Fans threw flowers on to the hearse, and the crowd erupted into applause and broke out into a rendition of Total Eclipse of the Heart. Mumbles was Tyler’s part-time home, as she split her time between Algarve in Portugal and a large Victorian house in Blackpill, near Mumbles, overlooking Swansea Bay. Tyler became renowned globally for her pop music hits, including Total Eclipse of the Heart and I Need a Hero. View image in fullscreen Bonnie Tyler fans (left-right) Melanie Smith, Melissa Smith and Carys Edwards in the Mumbles, Swansea, ahead of paying their respects to the late singer and watching the procession as she is transported back to her former home. Photograph: Eleanor Storey/PA Among those waiting to pay their respects to Tyler was Carys Edwards, 18, who said the singer was “an inspiration to everybody”. She told PA Media: “Her music touched a lot of people, especially me. I’m quite surprised how many people came here today, but then not as well, because she was such an icon. “She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans in Wales . “Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales, we loved her a lot. When we found out she passed away, it was such a heartbreak to all of us. We cried and everything.” View image in fullscreen A Welsh flag draped over the coffin of Bonnie Tyler. Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty Images Michael Bone, 58, and his partner Alan Hawkins, 54, travelled from Derby to watch the procession. “We thought it’d be nice to pay our respects,” said Bone. “For me personally, it’s because in my teens, her music was quite prolific. For me, it was her most iconic period in the 1980s.” Others were reported to have travelled from as far as Austria to witness the procession of Tyler’s coffin. Her other hits included It’s a Heartache and If You Were a Woman (And I Was a Man). She represented the UK in the 2013 Eurovision song contest in Malmö, Sweden, with the song Believe in Me, finishing in 19th place. A celebration of Tyler’s life is set to take place at Swansea Minster (Church of St Mary’s) on Monday 17 August. Only those with invitations will be allowed inside, but the service will be shown on a large screen in nearby St David’s Square – and members of the public can pay their respects. View image in fullscreen Bonnie Tyler. Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PA After the service, Tyler’s coffin will make a final journey through her home village of Skewen – followed by a private gathering strictly for family and friends. Tyler grew up in a council house in Skewen with five older siblings. “I class myself as a working-class girl, and I’ve never stopped working,” she told the Guardian in 2013. “I do an awful lot [of performances] because I feel other people would love to be offered what I’m offered.” In her memoir, she wrote fondly of Wales: “I may have done some extraordinary things … but in so many ways, I’m still that young girl from Wales, dancing around the piano with her family, and I always will be.” At the time of her death, then prime minister, Keir Starmer, said Tyler was an “iconic figure” and “one of Britain’s greatest recording artists”. Others who paid tribute to her included Catherine Zeta-Jones and Cliff Richard. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-votes-for-n.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MoKu The three-day election ends on Sunday evening Image: Tatiana Meel/REUTERS Advertisement Russians began casting ballots on Friday to elect a new lower house of parliament , kicking off a three-day vote that President Vladimir Putin's party is all but guaranteed to win. This is the first such election being held since Moscow sent troops to invade Ukraine in February 2022. Parties that support Putin's war in Ukraine are the only ones registered to run, and the opposition is barred from taking part. Russia's opposition party, Yabloko, was banished from the party list last month Image: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/picture alliance Despite expectations of Putin's easy win, the elections are widely being viewed as a referendum on the continuation of his military campaign — now in its fifth year. The polls are taking place at a time when public sentiment is starting to shift against the war over rising prices, internet crackdowns, fuel shortages and rumors of another mobilization drive following the elections. Meanwhile, Putin has called the vote a "collective contribution to Russia's victory against Ukraine. Vote for control More than 110 million Russians are eligible to vote for 450 members of the lower house of the Russian Parliament, known as the State Duma. Putin's United Russia party currently controls over two-thirds of the seats and is expected to retain its dominance, allowing it to continue the military campaign despite ebbing public support. The Kamchatka peninsula and Chukotka were the first of Russia's 11 time zones to begin voting on Friday. Polls will remain open until 1800 GMT on Sunday. Voting is being held for the first time in the Russia-occupied Ukrainian territories of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, against Kyiv's wishes. The Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, annexed by Moscow in 2014, is participating for the second time. While voters select their parliamentarians, members of regional parliaments will also be elected in eight regions. Edited by: Natalie Muller Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/poland-on-alert-am.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O8DI Amid a spate of violence this week, Tusk said 'spontaneous' attacks were 'inspired by online activity' [FILE: October 8] Image: Albert Zawada/PAP/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Authorities in Poland were meeting on Sunday to discuss a potential assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence ‌Minister ⁠Wladyslaw ⁠Kosiniak-Kamysz, Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Galecka said. The emergency meeting at the Internal Security Agency's (ABW) Counter-Terrorism Center was convened after police received information about a possible attack, Galecka said in a post on X. While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, the meeting comes as Polish authorities are on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week. Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months. What do we know about the school attacks in Poland? Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children. The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object. A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack. On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women. Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province. Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated. What did Tusk say about the attacks? On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online. "We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting. "In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued. The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment." Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online." The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories. Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.
